name: flux-redux
intent: Keep the application's shared presentation state in one store that changes only through dispatched action objects and pure reducers, so every UI update follows a single one-way path from user intent to new state and back to a re-render.
problem: Several components in different parts of the view tree need the same state and each one mutates its own copy or writes directly into the shared model: updates interleave, derived values such as counts, badges and validity drift away from the data they summarize, and no one can say which interaction changed what.
context: Client-side presentation layers of medium-to-large applications - web, mobile, desktop - where one state is read by many components, updates are frequent and their logic is non-trivial, state must survive navigation or a reload, and inspecting or replaying a session matters. It fits declarative view trees (React, Compose, SwiftUI, Blazor, iced) plus a runtime that can re-render from a new state value, and it is independent of any particular framework.
benefits: State changes follow one auditable path - view -> action -> reducer -> new state -> view - so 'who changed this, and when' has a single answer, and devtools can log, replay and time-travel the history.
Distant components read the same source of truth, so derived values cannot drift apart the way duplicated state or two-way bindings allow.
Reducers are pure functions over plain data: transitions are unit-testable without mounting a view, and the same reducer runs in the browser, in tests and on the server.
Views stay declarative functions of state - they subscribe to the slices they need and never write into each other - which decouples the component tree from where the state lives.
Middleware gives one seam for cross-cutting concerns (logging, persistence, async effects, undo) instead of re-implementing them in every component that touches shared state.
Serializable state plus an action stream enable persistence and hydration, offline queues, session replay and collaboration features that only need to ship actions.
tradeoffs: Indirection and ceremony: actions, action creators, reducers, selectors and a store replace a direct assignment - the Redux FAQ is explicit that it is 'not designed to be the shortest or fastest way to write code'.
One store is a coupling point and a bottleneck: unrelated features meet in one reducer tree, so slice boundaries become ongoing maintenance and a badly shared field silently links features.

Re-render cost depends on selector granularity: a component subscribed to too much state re-renders on every dispatch, and unstable selector results or inline object literals turn that into render storms.

The core discipline is unenforced in most languages: a reducer that mutates its input, or a view that mutates a snapshot, breaks identity-based change detection and history while the application still appears to work.

Asynchronous work has no single home: middleware, thunks, sagas and effects frameworks each add concepts, and classic Flux additionally needs dispatcher waitFor() ordering for inter-store dependencies.
Global state has gravity: transient UI state (hover, drafts, animation) migrates into the store and enlarges it, so every dispatch does more work than the feature needs.
Logging, persistence and time travel degrade quietly once non-serializable values (functions, class instances, DOM handles, dates) enter the state tree.

participants.responsibility: A plain, serializable description of something that happened - a type tag plus a payload. It is the only input a reducer accepts and the only thing a view may dispatch.
Builds an action from its arguments, giving callers a semantic API such as addTodo(text) and keeping action shapes out of the view code.
The single hub that receives every action and forwards it to the stores: Flux keeps it as a standalone dispatcher with waitFor() ordering, Redux folds the role into the store's dispatch function.
Holds the one state tree, runs the reducer when an action arrives and notifies subscribers; it exposes reads (getState plus selectors), dispatch and subscribe, and nothing else.
Pure function (state, action) -> nextState that decides how an action transforms the state, returns the previous state for actions it does not handle, and never mutates its input.
Intercepts dispatch to add cross-cutting behaviour (logging, async effects, persistence, undo) and may dispatch further actions or short-circuit the current one.
Derives the data a view needs from the state and composes or memoizes derived values, so components depend on a narrow, stable projection rather than the whole tree.

The view-side binding that subscribes to the store, maps state to props, passes values down and dispatches actions up - in Redux the connect/useSelector hooks, in Flux the controller-view at the top of a subtree.

use_cases: A single-page or mobile app whose screens, badges, filters and forms all read and write the same entities (todos, cart, inbox) that would otherwise be threaded through half the component tree as props.
Undo/redo, time travel or an audit trail: a serializable state plus an action log replays or rewinds a whole session (editors, drawing tools, wizards, trading UIs).
Offline-first and optimistic UIs: actions are queued and persisted while disconnected, replayed against the server, and the same reducers hydrate the state on load.
Server-rendered pages with rich client widgets: the store is preloaded from the server payload and then updated only through actions as the user interacts.
Large teams on one codebase: the action and reducer contract makes every state transition explicit in review, and the action list becomes the application's vocabulary.
Cross-platform products sharing one state layer: the same reducer tree runs on web, desktop and mobile while only the view layer is swapped.

Enterprise coordination layer: navigation, notifications, cache invalidation and dependent refreshes are owned by middleware or listener middleware, letting distant components coordinate without direct wiring (e.g., 900+ component apps where cross-cutting state changes would otherwise require prop threading).

Isomorphic/SSR apps with one dehydrated reducer tree: server produces the initial payload, client hydrates it and runs only actions; production deployments at scale (Yahoo Finance: 2M DAU, ~10 middlewares, ~3x RPS improvement).

Brownfield incremental adoption: introduced one feature or slice at a time alongside existing state, with containment of legacy flows; migration planning must account for both the technology migration and team upskilling.

Large multi-team codebases with slice ownership: uniform action vocabulary, DevTools auditing, and reducible dead state enable reviewable, measurable state management at scale (Shopify POS: 3,500 LOC of boilerplate deleted; 200k+ LOC dead code removed in a Redux/RxJS refactor).

RTK Query as a dedicated server-state layer: co-locate data fetching, caching, invalidation and optimistic updates inside the Redux store without mixing server payloads with UI state; derive all UI-facing projections in selectors.

Complex multi-step wizards or editors requiring undo/redo, savepoints and session replay: the Redux store serializes to localStorage or a DB, and the action log drives replay across sessions or devices.

Real-time collaborative UIs: actions are the shared vocabulary — concurrent edits resolve by replaying the operation stream, and the store's single-state model eliminates merge conflicts in the client state.

Angular enterprise applications via NgRx Store: an RxJS-powered single immutable state tree with dispatched actions, pure reducers, memoized selectors and Effects, composed with OnPush change detection - the Redux pattern as the Angular ecosystem's standard coordination layer.

Native GUIs without a web runtime: iced (Rust) drives cross-platform desktop apps through The Elm Architecture's loop - a State struct, a typed Message enum, an update function and a view function - showing the pattern survives outside JavaScript where the compiler enforces the message vocabulary.

Elm applications themselves (The Elm Architecture): Model + Update (Msg -> Model -> Model) + View (Model -> Html Msg) as the loop Redux was derived from - used wherever enforced purity and a compiler-checked message set matter more than ecosystem tooling.
avoid_when: The state is local and short-lived (a toggle, hover, one form): keep it in the component - a store adds indirection with no shared readers.
One screen owns the only copy of the data: lifting state up to the nearest common ancestor is the simpler answer.

The framework already ships a reducer-and-context mechanism (React useReducer + Context, Compose state holders, SwiftUI Observation) and the app is small: use the built-in system first - the Redux docs say not to adopt Redux until plain framework state becomes a problem.
Server state dominates (fetch, cache, invalidate, refetch): a data-fetching cache (React Query/SWR/Apollo-style) is the right tool - a Redux store is not a cache.

The data is high-frequency and ephemeral (pointer position, audio levels, per-frame simulation values): dispatch and re-render overhead make the store the wrong container; keep it in the loop and read it imperatively.
A few named states with explicit transitions describe the problem better: a state machine (state pattern, xstate-style) is clearer than an open-ended action log.
anti_patterns: Store-everything: transient UI state, server caches and derived values all hoisted into the global store, turning it into a god object that makes every dispatch expensive.
Mutating state inside a reducer (or mutating a snapshot in a view): change detection and time travel break while the app still appears to work.
Dispatching from render or derivation paths - selectors, effects that fire on every render - producing dispatch -> render -> dispatch feedback loops.
Using the store as a message bus: components dispatch action types that other components interpret as commands, encoding workflows in undocumented strings instead of in the model.
One giant switch reducer with no slice boundaries (and its inverse, many reducers fighting over one field), so every feature edit touches one unmergeable file.
Storing non-serializable values (class instances, functions, DOM nodes) so logging, persistence, hydration and time travel degrade silently.

Sequential multi-action dispatch for one user intent: a thunk or handler fires several low-level dispatches where one richer action and one reducer would do; intermediate states can be invalid and every dispatch triggers a subscriber round-trip.

Selector memoization that silently cannot cache: Date.now(), Math.random(), or inline object/array literals in the output selector return a new reference every time, forcing re-renders on every dispatch even when the relevant state slice is unchanged.

Deep-cloning the state tree on every transition (or storing derived values alongside source data) so that reference checks always fail and every dispatch re-renders all subscribers regardless of whether the slice changed.
Normalizing state beyond what queries actually need: deeply flattening data that is only ever read as a nested object adds conversion overhead on every read and write with no performance benefit.

createAsyncThunk without error handling: forgetting to handle rejected promises in extraReducers leaves the slice in a perpetual loading state; always add fulfilled/rejected cases or use unwrap() with try/catch at the call site.

Middleware ordering bugs: custom middleware that calls next() before or after async work, or that short-circuits dispatch without calling next(), silently swallows actions; log the middleware chain and verify dispatch call order in tests.

Store configured without serializability checks: omitting getDefaultMiddleware() or explicitly disabling the serializableStateMiddleware and immutableStateMiddleware dev checks allows non-serializable values to enter the state tree unnoticed, breaking history and hydration.

Entity adapter upsertOne does a shallow merge at the top entity level — nested objects inside the existing entity are fully overwritten by the upsert payload, silently discarding fields that are absent from the update; use merge + selective patch or a manual reducer case for partial nested updates.
design_principles: Single source of truth: each piece of shared state has exactly one owner, and nothing writes it out of band.
Unidirectional data flow: view -> action -> reducer -> new state -> view, with no second path back into the state.
Immutability: transitions produce new values, so change detection is identity comparison and history is preserved.
Command-query separation with explicit intent: actions name what happened, not what to set, and reducers decide the resulting state.
Separation of concerns: pure reducers keep the decisions, middleware and effects own I/O, views only render and dispatch.
Information hiding and dependency inversion: views depend on selectors and the dispatch contract, not on the store's internal shape.
best_practices: Model actions as events ('todos/todoAdded') with a single payload field rather than as setters, and name them with the domain's vocabulary.
Keep reducers pure and side-effect free; perform I/O, timers and randomness in middleware or effects that dispatch further actions.
Update immutably: copy the objects along the changed path, or rely on the language's persistent/immutable collections (or an Immer-style producer) instead of hand-copying deeply.
Split the state by domain slice, one reducer per slice, and compose them; normalize collections (byId plus ids) so each entity has one home.
Subscribe through narrow, memoized selectors with referentially stable results; never select the whole state in a leaf component.
Keep the state tree serializable and derive computed values in selectors instead of storing them.
Configure middleware and devtools once in a store factory, and export the factory so tests can build an isolated store.
Treat the store as application state, not as a server cache; fetched data lives in a cache, and only its UI-relevant projection belongs in the store.

Use Redux Toolkit for all Redux logic: configureStore, createSlice with Immer, createAsyncThunk, and createEntityAdapter — the legacy core package is considered obsolete for new code; RTK eliminates accidental mutation, the most common cause of Redux bugs.

Treat reducers as state machines: model each slice's finite states explicitly (idle, loading, success, failure) so that impossible state transitions are prevented and the UI can react to specific statuses rather than checking arbitrary field values.

Normalize complex nested or relational state using entity adapters ({ids, entities}); keep one authoritative record per entity and derive all views in memoized selectors instead of storing joined or filtered copies.

Call useSelector/useSelector multiple times for individual fields rather than returning one object; pass shallowEqual as the equality function when returning small flat objects, and always prefer stable references from memoized selectors over inline object or array literals.

Dispatch one action per user intent and let multiple reducers respond via extraReducers or listener middleware; avoid dispatching many sequential actions for a single interaction — batch them or model the logic as one richer event.

Move async logic into createAsyncThunk or listener middleware rather than into components; keep thunks free of nested dispatches that could be expressed as one action whose reducer handles the full state transition.

Adopt feature-folder layout with one slice file per feature (the ducks pattern); name state slices after the data they hold ({auth, posts, ui}), never after UI screens; export typed hooks (useAppSelector, useAppDispatch) from the store module.
Separate server state from client state: use RTK Query for all server data fetching, caching and cache invalidation — the Redux store should hold only UI-relevant projections, not raw API payloads.

Type actions with discriminated unions: define a literal type field ('type') and a payload union; TypeScript narrows the payload type in switch/if branches, eliminating the need for manual type casts and catching typos at compile time.

Normalize nested or relational state with createEntityAdapter ({ids, entities}); store each entity once with a stable id as key and derive all filtered/sorted views in memoized selectors instead of storing joined copies.

Prefer Reselect createSelector for all derived data; avoid returning new object/array literals from selectors as that defeats memoization and causes spurious re-renders; structure selectors as a pipeline of map/filter over normalized ids.

Test reducers as pure state machines: supply (state, action) pairs and assert the next state — no store, no components; test happy path, unknown-action passthrough, and error/loading state transitions for every slice.

Adopt feature-folder layout (ducks pattern): co-locate slice, selectors, thunks and tests per feature rather than splitting by function type across the entire codebase; name exports after the feature domain, not the file type.

Export typed store hooks (useAppSelector, useAppDispatch) from the store module and use them exclusively in components; this gates all component-store coupling in one place and makes store refactoring tractable.
Batch UI updates with React 18 startTransition or unstable_batchedUpdates when dispatching from event handlers that may trigger multiple state changes, reducing render commit overhead.
Use createListenerMiddleware or a custom middleware for cross-cutting concerns (webSocket feeds, notification bridges, analytics) instead of ad-hoc store subscriptions scattered across components.
Keep action types namespaced ('domain/eventName') and avoid generic names like 'SET_DATA'; namespaced types prevent collisions as the action vocabulary grows across teams and features.
